claim: FSSAI ordered all Indian states on March 7, 2023 to conduct a special enforcement drive against non-compliant nutraceuticals under the Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2022, with action reports required by March 31, 2023.
stance_target: FSSAI regulatory enforcement for supplements in India
quoted_support: FSSAI ordered on March 7 for all states to carry out a 'special enforcement drive' to check for product compliance and to 'take strict action against any incidence of violation by the FBOs (food business operators)'.

claim: Many imported US vitamin C supplements sold in India contain 500mg-1,000mg per serving, far exceeding FSSAI's permitted RDI of 80mg (men) and 65mg (women) — and such products are legally classified as medicines in India requiring doctor's prescription.
stance_target: Dosage compliance of imported supplements in India
quoted_support: In India, the permitted RDI of vitamin C is 80mg for men and 65mg for women... However, several products in the retail market, mostly imported from the US, contain 500mg or 1,000mg of vitamin C... Such products are regulated as medicines and can only be made available via doctor's prescription.

claim: Common nutraceutical non-compliance in India includes: protein adulteration, mismatch between claimed and actual bioactive amounts, vegetarian-labeled products with non-vegetarian ingredients, and use of non-permitted ingredient forms such as synthetic astaxanthin.
stance_target: Types of supplement adulteration in India
quoted_support: Some examples of non-compliance, he said, were how nutraceuticals with the vegetarian logo were found to contain non-vegetarian ingredients, how certain products, such as protein, were adulterated. Another problem is the mismatch in the amount of bioactive claimed and the actual amount detected.
